citation.title: Driving Fatalities on US Presidential Election Days: A Reanalysis

standing_assumptions:
The article is a three-page short report (BMC Research Notes (2016) 9:341; the first page is unnumbered and the others are headed ‘Page 2 of 3’ and ‘Page 3 of 3’, so the printed page number equals the PDF page number). It states no theorem, proposition or lemma, displays no formula and gives no proof; its only formal objects are the relative-risk statistic, the empirical null distribution with its two-tailed $P$ value, and the Wald-type interval, all defined in words. The setting, as printed (read from the page images):
(S1) The statistic (Methods, p. 1): “RT used data collected from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System over the years 1975–2006. The primary analysis computed a relative risk by taking the number of persons in fatal crashes during election hours on presidential election days from 1976 through 2004, and comparing this to the average of the number of individuals in fatal crashes during the same hours one week before and one week after. We henceforth refer to RT’s test statistic—the risk relative to the same time period in the previous and following week—as the RR (relative risk).” (footnote mark 1) “Throughout, in the interest of replication, we will use RT’s test statistic as our basis for inference.” “Following a finding reported in a later article by Redelmeier and Tibshirani [2], we estimate RRs during non-election hours as well as during the full 24 h on presidential election days.”
(S2) The empirical null distribution, the $P$ value and the interval (Methods, Page 2 of 3): “To assess statistical significance, we estimated RRs for the 100 Tuesdays before and after presidential election days. (We restrict ourselves to Tuesdays as all United States presidential elections are held on Tuesdays, thus conditioning on any day-of-week effects.) Using these 200 RRs, we constructed an empirical null distribution, with non-parametric two-tailed $P$ values computed as the proportion of RRs more extreme (i.e., RR greater or 1/RR smaller) than that of presidential election days. This procedure tests against the null hypothesis that election days have an RR consistent with being drawn randomly from the distribution of Tuesdays [3]. We further calculated 95 % Wald-type confidence intervals (CIs) under a normal approximation using the standard deviation of the empirical null distribution as an estimate of the standard error. Throughout, we consider only presidential elections from 1980 through 2008, as data were not available before 1975 or after 2012, precluding estimation for all Tuesdays surrounding the 1976 or 2012 elections.”
(S3) Fig. 1 (Page 2 of 3): three panels, titled “Relative Risk of Driving Fatalities (Election Hours)”, “Relative Risk of Driving Fatalities (Non-Election Hours)” and “Relative Risk of Driving Fatalities (Full 24 Hours)”, each with vertical axis “Relative Risk” (ticks 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.25, 1.50) and horizontal axis “Weeks Before/After Presidential Election Day” (ticks −100 to 100 in steps of 10). Caption: “Fig. 1 Relative risk (RR) estimates for presidential election days and the 100 preceding and following Tuesdays. Red dots indicate RRs for all Tuesdays. Black circles indicate RRs and black dashed lines indicate RR and 1/RR for presidential election days. The proportion of red dots outside black dashed lines is equivalent to the reported non-parametric $P$ value”.
(S4) The main results (Results, Page 3 of 3): “We estimate an RR for election hours during presidential elections from 1980 to 2008 of 1.17 (non-parametric $P = 0.070$, Wald-type 95 % CI [0.99,1.35]).” “Furthermore, we estimate an equally strong negative effect of presidential elections on driving fatalities during non-election hours on election days, with an RR = 0.83 (non-parametric $P = 0.085$, Wald-type 95 % CI [0.60,1.06]). When we included the full 24 h on election days, we found no evidence of an effect of presidential elections, with an RR = 1.04 (non-parametric $P = 0.570$, Wald-type 95 % CI [0.89,1.20]). Figure 1 shows the RRs for election days and the surrounding 200 Tuesdays.” (footnote mark 2).
(S5) Alternative null windows (footnote 2, Page 3 of 3): “We also computed $P$ values for alternative time periods for the null distribution, namely for the surrounding 12, 25 and 50 Tuesdays. For the 12 surrounding Tuesday specifications, we find for election hours, non-election hours, and the full day, respective $P$ values of 0.04, 0.04, and 0.46. For 25 Tuesdays, we find respectively 0.06, 0.02, and 0.42. For 50 Tuesdays, we find respectively 0.05, 0.08, and 0.47.”
Not in the paper or the staged sources: the FARS counts, the plotted RR values as numbers, and any code (the staged manifest records the FARS data as unavailable and no replication code). Every statement below about which reference Tuesdays are ‘more extreme’ is therefore a statement about the published Fig. 1, not about the source data.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 2, third sentence, first value (the election-hours non-parametric P value when the null distribution is the 25 Tuesdays before and the 25 after election day, printed 0.06), corrected against Fig. 1, top panel: two of the fifty reference RRs are outside the dashed lines, which gives 2/50 = 0.04, and 0.06 requires three
canonical_claim.location: Page 3 of 3 (PDF p. 3), footnote 2; Fig. 1, top panel (‘Election Hours’) and caption, Page 2 of 3 (PDF p. 2); the P value is defined in Methods, Page 2 of 3 (PDF p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; footnote 2, Page 3 of 3] “We also computed $P$ values for alternative time periods for the null distribution, namely for the surrounding 12, 25 and 50 Tuesdays. For the 12 surrounding Tuesday specifications, we find for election hours, non-election hours, and the full day, respective $P$ values of 0.04, 0.04, and 0.46. For 25 Tuesdays, we find respectively 0.06, 0.02, and 0.42. For 50 Tuesdays, we find respectively 0.05, 0.08, and 0.47.” The value at issue is the first of the third sentence: the election-hours $P$ value for the 25-Tuesday window, printed 0.06. [Printed; Fig. 1 caption, Page 2 of 3] “The proportion of red dots outside black dashed lines is equivalent to the reported non-parametric $P$ value”.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P038-N005, verbatim] “Reconcile footnote 2 and Figure 1 against the final data. If Figure 1 is correct, replace the first 25-week value, 0.06, with 0.04. If 0.06 is the verified final-data result, correct the figure to show the requisite third tail point and any other affected plotted quantities; its identity cannot be determined from the staged sources.” Under the first branch the third sentence of footnote 2 reads: “For 25 Tuesdays, we find respectively 0.04, 0.02, and 0.42.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Notation (not in the paper). Fix one time-of-day category (here election hours). Let $R > 0$ be the election-day RR and, for each integer $w$ with $1 \le |w| \le 100$, let $r_w > 0$ be the RR of the Tuesday $w$ weeks after ($w > 0$) or $-w$ weeks before ($w < 0$) election day. For an integer $m$ with $1 \le m \le 100$ put $W_m = \{w \in \mathbb{Z} : 1 \le |w| \le m\}$, so that $|W_m| = 2m$ and week $0$ is not in $W_m$. Call $r_w$ more extreme than $R$ when it lies outside the dashed lines of Fig. 1, that is, when $r_w < \min(R, 1/R)$ or $r_w > \max(R, 1/R)$. Put $T = \{w : r_w \text{ is more extreme than } R\}$, $k_m = |T \cap W_m|$ and $$P_m = \frac{k_m}{2m}.$$ The main specification is $m = 100$ (200 RRs); footnote 2 is read as $m = 12, 25, 50$ (24, 50 and 100 RRs). A two-decimal number $v$ is the rounding of $x$ when $v - \tfrac{1}{200} \le x < v + \tfrac{1}{200}$.
(i) [The value the figure gives] For every $R > 0$ and every family $(r_w)_{w \in W_{25}}$ of positive reals of which exactly two are more extreme than $R$ (that is, $k_{25} = 2$), $$P_{25} = \frac{2}{50} = \frac{1}{25} = 0.04 .$$
(ii) [What the printed value requires] For every integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le 50$: $\frac{k}{50} = \frac{6}{100}$ if and only if $k = 3$; $\frac{k}{50}$ rounds to $0.06$ if and only if $k = 3$; and $\frac{k}{50}$ rounds to $0.04$ if and only if $k = 2$. Consequently $P_{25}$ equals (equivalently, rounds to) the printed $0.06$ if and only if exactly three of the fifty reference RRs are more extreme than $R$, and equals $0.04$ if and only if exactly two are. The two published outputs (footnote 2: $0.06$; Fig. 1: two reference points outside the lines) therefore cannot both be right; they differ by $\frac{6}{100} - \frac{1}{25} = \frac{1}{50}$, one tail point in fifty.
(iii) [The 12-Tuesday value agrees with the same figure] $k_m \le k_{m'}$ whenever $m \le m'$. If $T \cap W_{25} = \{-14, 7\}$ (the two tail points of the election-hours panel), then $k_{12} = 1$ and $k_{25} = 2$, so $P_{12} = \frac{1}{24}$, which rounds to the printed $0.04$ because $\frac{35}{1000} \le \frac{1}{24} < \frac{45}{1000}$, while $P_{25} = 0.04$ and does not round to $0.06$.
(iv) [Counting the election day itself does not reconcile them] If the election-day point were counted as one more extreme observation among $2m + 1$ points, the 25-Tuesday value would be $\frac{k_{25} + 1}{51} = \frac{3}{51} = \frac{1}{17}$, which rounds to $0.06$ because $\frac{55}{1000} \le \frac{1}{17} < \frac{65}{1000}$; but the 12-Tuesday value would be $\frac{k_{12} + 1}{25} = \frac{2}{25} = 0.08$, which does not round to the printed $0.04$. So with $T \cap W_{25} = \{-14, 7\}$ neither convention gives both printed election-hours values ($0.04$ for 12 Tuesdays and $0.06$ for 25).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The RR: standing assumption (S1). The empirical null distribution and the two-tailed $P$ value: (S2), in particular “Using these 200 RRs, we constructed an empirical null distribution, with non-parametric two-tailed $P$ values computed as the proportion of RRs more extreme (i.e., RR greater or 1/RR smaller) than that of presidential election days.” (Methods, Page 2 of 3). The rule shown in the figure: “Black circles indicate RRs and black dashed lines indicate RR and 1/RR for presidential election days. The proportion of red dots outside black dashed lines is equivalent to the reported non-parametric $P$ value” (Fig. 1 caption, Page 2 of 3). The alternative windows: footnote 2, standing assumption (S5).
Not in the paper (the readings and the data that the statement uses).
(a) ‘More extreme’. The Methods parenthesis “(i.e., RR greater or 1/RR smaller)” does not by itself state two tails (finding P038-E002, rated a clarity note); the rule used here is the caption's: a reference RR $r$ is counted when it lies outside the two dashed lines drawn at the election-day RR $R$ and at its reciprocal, $r < \min(R, 1/R)$ or $r > \max(R, 1/R)$, with strict inequalities (‘outside’). For positive numbers this is the same condition as $|\log r| > |\log R|$ and as $\max(r, 1/r) > \max(R, 1/R)$ (validator, _batch/P038-B01/work/derivations.md); these equivalent forms are not part of the target. The paper does not say how ties are treated, and none occurs among the points at issue.
(b) The windows. Methods uses “the 100 Tuesdays before and after” and counts “200 RRs”; footnote 2's “surrounding 12, 25 and 50 Tuesdays” is read the same way, as that many Tuesdays on each side of election day, giving 24, 50 and 100 reference RRs with the election day (week 0) excluded (finding P038-N004, rated a clarity note). The footnote's own numbers require this reading: with 25 RRs in all, every attainable proportion is a multiple of $\frac{1}{25} = 0.04$ and none rounds to the printed 0.06, 0.02 or 0.42, whereas with 50 RRs these are $\frac{3}{50}$, $\frac{1}{50}$ and $\frac{21}{50}$. The election-day RR $R$ and the reference RRs $r_w$ are those of the main specification (elections from 1980 through 2008); only the set of reference weeks changes with the window.
(c) The figure's data. The RR values are not printed as numbers; the statement uses only which reference points lie outside the dashed lines. In the election-hours panel of Fig. 1 the dashed lines are at the election-day RR (printed 1.17) and at its reciprocal, and among the 50 reference points at weeks −25 to −1 and 1 to 25 exactly two have their centres outside the lines: week −14 (below the lower line) and week +7 (above the upper line). The point at week +6 touches the lower line and has its centre inside; the election-day point (week 0, circled) lies on the upper line by construction and is not a reference point. This is read from the embedded raster of Fig. 1 (1595 × 1740 pixels; in the top panel the dashed lines are at rows 170 and 274, week 0 is at x = 872.5 and a week is 6.55 pixels) by the validator (P038-N005/v1/artifact/check.py, check.out, top25_annotated.png), was reproduced by the recheck with a different colour mask (P038-N005/recheck-v1/independent_check.py), and was recounted when this list was fixed.
canonical_claim.note: P038-N005 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): one of the nine robustness $P$ values of footnote 2 (election hours, 25 Tuesdays on each side: printed 0.06) disagrees with the paper's own Fig. 1 (2 of 50 reference points outside the lines, 0.04), so one of the two published outputs carries a wrong number. Sol's verdict: confirmed in part, upheld on re-run; the internal inconsistency is confirmed, and which of the two outputs is the wrong one is not established (the external check found the thesis the article is based on but could not read its full text). This is the only target for the work and a marginal one: a finding about a reported number in an empirical report, included because the author's instruction covers every confirmed mathematical error at any severity and because the correction is exact arithmetic on a count that the paper's own figure displays under the paper's own stated rule. What a Lean statement can certify is (i) to (iv): the relation between a tail count and the $P$ value, for arbitrary positive RRs, and the rounding facts. It cannot certify the hypothesis $k_{25} = 2$ (equivalently $T \cap W_{25} = \{-14, 7\}$), which is a reading of the published raster and must appear as a hypothesis, nor that the figure and not the footnote reflects the final FARS data. The corrected value 0.04 is therefore conditional on the figure being right; under the other branch of Sol's repair the footnote stands and the figure needs a third tail point, which by (ii) is exactly what 0.06 requires. Under the figure-based repair the 25-Tuesday election-hours value moves from above to below 0.05; no main-text number, interval or conclusion uses it (the main election-hours value is $P = 0.070$). (iv) records the validator's remark that counting the election day gives 3/51, which rounds to 0.06; the validator does not offer this as the cause of the discrepancy, and it fails at 12 Tuesdays. No rounding tie arises ($k/50$ is a multiple of 0.02, and $\frac{1}{24}$, $\frac{1}{17}$ are not at a boundary), so the half-up convention in the statement is immaterial. Why there is nothing else on the list: no headline claim of this work (P038-H1 to P038-H7) is a mathematical statement, all being empirical estimates or interpretive conclusions, so there is no headline target; the other confirmed findings (P038-E001, P038-E002, P038-N004) are rated clarity notes, not errors, and get no target of their own, though (a) and (b) of definitions_needed fix the readings that two of them concern; P038-N003 is undetermined and P038-N001, P038-N002 are not confirmed. The finding is Minor, so there is no result_touched_by_finding target, and the validator gave a recalculation from the source and not a counterexample. When this list was fixed, the equalities and rounding claims of (i) to (iv) and of (b) were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic, and the tail count within 25 weeks was recounted from the embedded figure (saturated red ink beyond the dashed-line bands only at weeks −14, 0 and +7).
